title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a viable source of feedback for complex writing tasks, specifically argumentative essay writing, and how the quality of AI-generated feedback compares with peer-generated feedback. The authors frame the study around a practical educational problem: teachers often struggle to provide timely, high-quality feedback on essays, especially in large classes, and peer feedback can also be inconsistent because students may lack sufficient expertise or feedback skills. The study asks two main questions: whether ChatGPT-generated and peer-generated feedback differ in quality, and whether essay quality is related to the quality of feedback produced by either source.

The intervention involved an online argumentative essay writing module delivered through the Brightspace platform. In week one, students individually wrote essays on course-related controversial topics. In week two, students provided asynchronous written peer feedback on two peers’ essays using a structured prompt through the FeedbackFruits tool, while the researchers also submitted the same essays to ChatGPT using a closely matched prompt to generate AI feedback. The researchers then analyzed both the essays and the feedback using established coding schemes that assessed essay quality and feedback features such as affective, cognitive, and constructive elements.

The study took place at a Dutch university specializing in life sciences and involved 74 graduate students in food sciences. The context was fully online and focused on higher education rather than K-12. Quantitative analyses included MANCOVA to compare peer and ChatGPT feedback quality and Spearman correlations to examine relationships between essay quality and feedback quality.

The main conclusion is that peer feedback was overall higher quality than ChatGPT feedback, largely because peers were better at identifying problems in essays, whereas ChatGPT was stronger at descriptive feedback such as summarizing essay content. The authors argue that ChatGPT may still be useful as a complementary feedback source rather than a replacement for peer or teacher feedback. They also found no overall significant relationship between essay quality and the quality of feedback generated by peers or ChatGPT. The paper emphasizes the promise of AI-supported feedback while noting important limitations regarding sample scope, short duration, and lack of evidence on how students used the feedback for revision.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical comparison study with structured coding and statistical analysis, but it is exploratory, non-K-12, from a single graduate course, and not a randomized impact evaluation of student outcomes. It provides some methodological rigor but does not meet stronger causal evidence standards.
impact_tier_rationale: The study finds small differences in feedback characteristics between ChatGPT and peer feedback, but it does not measure downstream learning gains, revision quality, or independent writing outcomes. As a result, educational impact is unclear rather than clearly positive or negative.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT-generated written feedback on graduate students’ argumentative essays, using a fixed prompt to provide 250–350 word feedback about argument elements, problems, and improvement suggestions.

finding.finding_summary: In a comparison of ChatGPT-generated versus peer-generated feedback on argumentative essays, ChatGPT produced significantly more descriptive feedback, while peers were significantly better at identifying problems in essays. Reported effects were small: description F(1,146)=3.25, p<0.05, η²=0.03; identification F(1,146)=4.38, p<0.01, η²=0.02; no significant differences were found for affective, justification, or constructive feedback dimensions. The study did not test revision gains or independent post-writing performance, so literacy improvement from AI feedback was not established.
finding.measure: Coded quality of essay feedback on argumentative writing (affective, cognitive: description/identification/justification, and constructive components) using rubric-based ratings
finding.effect_size: η²=0.03 for description; η²=0.02 for identification
finding.std_deviation: Peer description SD=0.29; ChatGPT description SD=0.00; Peer identification SD=0.49; ChatGPT identification SD=0.70

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT could potentially complement peer feedback and help reduce teacher feedback workload in large-enrolment writing contexts, but this was not directly tested empirically. No time, cost, productivity, or workload outcome measures were collected, so any operational benefit remains inferential rather than demonstrated.
finding.measure: Not directly measured; discussion-based implication about scalability and teacher workload reduction
